title: Group Chat & E2E Encryption
description: Design group message fan-out, implement end-to-end encryption with Signal's Double Ratchet protocol, prekey bundles, forward secrecy, and group key management.

segments.text: Group chat fan-out has two approaches. Write to each member's inbox: sender posts one message, server writes N copies to N member inboxes. Simple reads but write amplification — a group of five hundred members means five hundred writes per message. Shared inbox: one write, all members read from the same location. Less writes but read contention.

WhatsApp uses per-member inbox for small groups and shared inbox for broadcast lists. The threshold is typically around two hundred fifty members. Below that, write amplification is manageable. Above that, shared inbox with per-member read cursors is more efficient. WeChat groups cap at five hundred members partly for this reason.

End-to-end encryption means only the sender and recipient can read messages — not even the server. This is non-negotiable for privacy-focused messaging. Without E2E, a compromised server exposes all message history. WhatsApp enabled E2E for two billion users in 2016, and Signal's protocol is the gold standard.

Signal's Double Ratchet combines two mechanisms. The Diffie-Hellman ratchet generates new shared secrets with every message exchange — if one key is compromised, future messages remain secure. The symmetric ratchet derives per-message keys from the shared secret. Together, they provide both forward and backward secrecy.

Prekey bundles solve the offline problem. Alice wants to message Bob who's offline. Bob pre-uploads one hundred one-time prekeys to the server. Alice grabs one, combines it with Bob's identity key and her own keys to establish a shared secret. When Bob comes online, he can derive the same secret and decrypt Alice's message. Each prekey is used once then discarded.

Forward secrecy means compromising today's key doesn't decrypt yesterday's messages. But here's the challenge: if you rotate keys with every message, how do you handle a message that arrives out of order? Think about this edge case.
segments.thought_prompt: If encryption keys rotate per message, how do you decrypt a message that arrives out of order?

segments.text: Group E2E encryption is harder. You can't do pairwise encryption for a group of one hundred — that's N-squared key exchanges. Signal uses Sender Keys: each group member generates a sender key, distributes it to all members via pairwise encrypted channels. Messages are encrypted once with the sender key, not N times. When someone leaves, all sender keys must be rotated.

Group key rotation on member removal is critical. If someone leaves the group, they still have the old sender keys and could decrypt future messages if keys aren't rotated. WhatsApp rotates all sender keys when any member leaves. For large groups, this means redistributing keys to all remaining members — expensive but necessary for security.

E2E encryption has tradeoffs. Server-side search is impossible — messages are encrypted blobs. Spam detection requires client-side classifiers. Message backup requires encrypting the backup separately. And key verification — how do you know you're talking to the real person? Signal uses safety numbers that users manually compare, but most people never do.
You're designing an enterprise chat with groups up to ten thousand members, E2E encryption requirement, and full-text search. These requirements conflict. How would you architect this?
segments.thought_prompt: Design enterprise chat with 10K-member groups, E2E encryption, and full-text search. Resolve the conflicts.

segments.text: Group chat requires choosing between per-member inbox and shared inbox based on group size. E2E encryption with the Double Ratchet protocol provides forward secrecy, prekey bundles enable offline messaging, and Sender Keys make group encryption efficient. The Staff-level insight: E2E encryption is a feature that constrains your entire architecture — embrace those constraints early.
